chief_complaint: numbness and burning stocking distribution, Romberg positive
hpi_details: 62-year-old male with a 15-year history of poorly controlled Type 2 Diabetes presents to the PM&R clinic for progressive, bilateral, burning pain and numbness in his feet up to the mid-calves (stocking distribution). He reports worsening balance, feeling unsteady when walking in the dark.
ideas: He thinks poor blood circulation and clogged arteries from his diabetes are starving his feet of blood and oxygen.
concerns: He is terrified that the numbness means he will develop an undetected foot ulcer and end up needing an amputation like a friend from church.
expectations: He hopes to get a prescription nerve pain medication to quiet the burning at night and advice on protective shoes so he doesn't stumble in the dark.
pmh: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, 15-year history, poorly controlled

clinical_knowledge.topic: Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Management includes glycemic optimization and foot protection. Consider neuropathic-pain medication after reviewing comorbidities, renal function, interactions, and fall risk; prescribe balance rehabilitation and protective footwear according to functional and foot-risk assessment.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: numbness and burning stocking distribution, Romberg positive

Key HPI features: 62-year-old male with a 15-year history of poorly controlled Type 2 Diabetes presents to the PM&R clinic for progressive, bilateral, burning pain and numbness in his feet up to the mid-calves (stocking distribution). He reports worsening balance, feeling unsteady when walking in the dark.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy.
Relevant background/PMH: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, 15-year history, poorly controlled
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Soft tissue strain without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe progressive motor deficit.
management_principles: Optimize diabetes care and foot protection; consider neuropathic-pain medication only after individualized review of comorbidities, renal function, interactions, and fall risk.

Refer for balance and gait rehabilitation when unsteadiness or falls are present, and obtain prompt specialist assessment for motor-predominant, rapidly progressive, asymmetric, or atypical neuropathy.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 62M with chronic Type 2 Diabetes presenting with symmetric distal paresthesias, allodynia, and sensory ataxia.
reference_soap.objective: Neurological exam: Loss of protective sensation bilaterally to 10g monofilament. Absent ankle jerks. Decreased vibratory sense and proprioception at the great toes. Positive Romberg sign (loses balance with eyes closed).
reference_soap.assessment: Diabetic Sensorimotor Polyneuropathy with sensory ataxia.
reference_soap.plan: Optimize diabetes care and foot protection. Consider neuropathic-pain medication after individualized review of comorbidities, renal function, interactions, and fall risk. Refer for balance and gait rehabilitation because of unsteadiness; obtain prompt specialist assessment for motor-predominant, rapidly progressive, asymmetric, or atypical neuropathy. Consider diabetic therapeutic footwear based on foot-risk assessment.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy
Implement an individualized neuropathy plan with fall prevention, foot protection, and medication selection guided by patient risk factors

teaching.one_liner: Physical medicine presentation involving numbness and burning stocking distribution, Romberg positive.

must_ask.say: When did the numbness and burning start, and did it begin in your feet before moving up your legs?
How long have you had diabetes, and how well controlled has your blood sugar been?
Have you felt unsteady on your feet or had any falls, especially in the dark?

must_ask.objective: Loss of protective sensation / foot screening
must_ask.say: Have you noticed any sores, cuts, or wounds on your feet that you didn't feel happen?
Is the pain worse at night, even when something light like your bedsheet touches your feet?

history.answer: Doctor, both of my feet have been feeling numb and burning, and it seems to be getting worse.
It is mostly tingling, numbness, and an intense burning feeling; my legs don't feel paralyzed, just unsteady.
It is in both feet equally, going up to about my mid-calves like I am wearing burning socks, but my hands feel completely normal.
It began very gradually about a year or two ago in my toes, and it has slowly crept up my legs over the last several months.
I feel clumsy and unsteady when walking, especially at night in the dark or on uneven ground because I cannot feel where my feet are.
The burning pain gets much worse at night when I am resting in bed.
Yes, even the light bedsheet touching my feet feels irritating and painfully sensitive.
No, I have no neck stiffness, back pain, or pain shooting down from my spine.
No, I haven't had any slurred speech, drooping on one side of my face, sudden vision changes, or dizziness.
No, my bowel and bladder habits are completely normal, and I have no numbness in my groin or buttocks.
No shortness of breath, drooping eyelids, double vision, or trouble chewing or swallowing.
No, I haven't noticed any muscle twitching, cramping, or shrinking in my leg muscles.
No, I haven't had any cold, flu, diarrhea, or stomach bugs recently.
I have had type 2 diabetes for about 15 years, and my control has not been good lately; my last hemoglobin A1c was around 9.2 percent.
I eat a balanced diet with plenty of meat and fish, and I have never had stomach or intestinal surgery.
No fever, chills, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss.
I try to look at my feet occasionally, and I haven't seen any open cuts, blisters, or ulcers.
No, I work at a desk and don't do repetitive wrist motions, prolonged squatting, or resting on my elbows.
I figured my circulation must be getting really poor and blood just isn't reaching my feet anymore because of my diabetes.
A friend of mine lost his toes to diabetes, and I'm terrified that this numbness means my feet are going to get infected and have to be amputated.
I'm hoping you can give me something to stop that terrible burning so I can sleep, and tell me if I need special shoes to keep from falling.
Other than my type 2 diabetes, I haven't been diagnosed with any other chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and have never stayed overnight in a hospital.
I take metformin 1000 milligrams twice a day, and I don't take any supplements or over-the-counter painkillers regularly.
I don't have any known allergies to medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink an occasional beer when socializing, maybe once or twice a month.
I work as an office accountant and live in a single-story house with my wife.
My mother also had type 2 diabetes, but there is no family history of early heart disease, stroke, or inherited nerve disorders.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 128/82 mmHg, heart rate is 74 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate is 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, and temperature is 36.6°C.
Skin on both feet is intact without erythema, calluses, ulcerations, or signs of infection.
Bilateral dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ and symmetric, with capillary refill under 2 seconds.
Cranial nerves II through XII are intact, with symmetric facial movements, clear speech, and normal visual fields.
Normal muscle bulk without atrophy or fasciculations; muscle strength is 5/5 across all proximal and distal muscle groups in upper and lower extremities.

Loss of protective sensation bilaterally to 10g monofilament; decreased pinprick, light touch, and vibratory sense in a symmetric stocking distribution up to mid-calves, with impaired proprioception at the great toes.
Biceps, triceps, and patellar reflexes are 2+ bilaterally, while Achilles reflexes are absent bilaterally; Babinski sign is negative bilaterally.
Normal finger-to-nose testing, mildly wide-based gait, and positive Romberg sign with pronounced unsteadiness upon closing eyes.
No cervical or lumbar spine tenderness, and straight-leg raise test is negative bilaterally.
